## Digital Marketing Agency in Pune: How to Read Your Google Ads Search Terms Report and Stop Paying for the Wrong Clicks

If you run Google Search ads for a local or service business, the single most useful report in your account is the search terms report. It lists the actual phrases people typed before they saw and clicked your ad, which are often quite different from the keywords you chose. Reviewing it every week, and adding negative keywords for the phrases that will never become customers, is the most direct way to stop paying for the wrong clicks. A good digital marketing agency in Pune does this as a routine task and shows you the results; if yours does not, this guide will help you ask for it.

This article is for business owners and marketing managers who spend on Google Ads themselves or through an agency and want to understand what is happening to the budget. It explains what the report shows, how to read it, how negative keywords and their match types work, how to build lists that you can reuse, what changes with broader match types and automated campaign types, and a weekly routine you can follow. It does not promise a particular saving: how much of a budget is wasted on irrelevant searches depends on the account, the industry and how it was built.

## What the search terms report is, and why it matters

When you bid on a keyword in Google Ads, the match type decides how closely a search must resemble that keyword before your ad can appear. Google's own help pages describe the search terms report as the place to see the searches that triggered your ads, and as a source of ideas for new keywords and for negative keywords ([Google Ads Help: negative keyword ideas from the search terms report](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/7102466)).

The gap between "the keyword I bid on" and "the search someone typed" is where budget is lost. Take a Pune interior designer bidding on "interior designer pune". Searches that may trigger the ad include "interior designer jobs pune", "interior design course pune" and "free interior design software". None of those people are likely to hire you. They are paying clicks all the same.

### What the report shows

For each search term you can see, among other columns, the impressions, clicks, cost, conversions and the keyword and match type that triggered the ad. This is the only place in the account where the real language of your potential customers, and of people who are not potential customers, is visible.

### What it does not show

Google has said that, for privacy reasons, some search terms are not shown individually in the report, typically low-volume queries. So the report is a large sample of what is happening, not a complete record. Do not assume that cleaning up every visible term means the account is clean, and do not trust any figure that claims to know exactly how much budget is wasted. Check Google's current help documentation for the details of what is shown, because the rules have changed over time.

## Reading the report: a practical method

Open the report for a period long enough to contain meaningful data, such as the last 30 days, and sort by cost, highest first. Start with the terms that have spent the most money, because that is where the largest savings or the largest lessons are.

### Sort every term into one of four buckets

1. **Right searches that convert.** Terms that led to enquiries, calls or sales. These can often be added as exact or phrase match keywords so you control bids and ads for them directly.
2. **Right searches with no conversions yet.** The intent looks right but nothing has happened. Leave these, and give them enough data before judging them. A handful of clicks is rarely enough to condemn a keyword.
3. **Wrong intent.** Job seekers, students, people looking for free or DIY solutions, people looking for a different service, competitors' staff. These are candidates for negative keywords.
4. **Wrong geography or wrong product.** Searches for a city you do not serve, a service you do not offer or a brand you do not sell.

The temptation is to treat everything without a conversion as wasted. Resist it. Many accounts have conversion tracking that is incomplete, for example phone calls that are not recorded, so a term that looks unproductive may have produced calls you cannot see. Check that tracking works before cutting terms on the basis of conversion data. Our guide to [call tracking for Google Ads leads](/blog/call-tracking-google-ads-india) explains how to close that gap, and our article on [why cheap leads are not always good leads](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-lead-quality-offline-conversions-2026) explains how to tie ad clicks to sales outcomes.

### Look for themes, not just single terms

Reading one query at a time is slow and misleading. Look for words that recur across many irrelevant queries: "jobs", "salary", "course", "training", "free", "diy", "pdf", "meaning", "definition", "login". A single negative keyword can then remove hundreds of future variants.

Equally important, look for the opposite: recurring words in converting searches that you have not yet targeted. Customers will often use terms you would never have guessed, and those are cheap and valuable additions.

## What negative keywords are and how the match types work

A negative keyword tells Google not to show your ad for searches containing a particular word or phrase. They can be set at the ad group level, the campaign level, in shared lists applied to several campaigns, and in some campaign types at the account level.

### The three match types, with examples

Negative keywords have their own match types, and they behave differently from positive keywords. This catches many people out.

- **Negative broad match.** The ad will not show if the search contains all the words of the negative keyword, in any order. If your negative is `free course`, a search for "interior design course free" is blocked, but a search for "interior design course" is not, because the word "free" is missing.
- **Negative phrase match.** The ad will not show if the search contains the words in that exact order, possibly with other words before or after. A negative of `"free course"` blocks "free course interior design" but not "course for free".
- **Negative exact match.** The ad will not show only when the search is precisely that term, with nothing added. A negative of `[interior design jobs]` blocks that exact search and leaves "interior design jobs in pune" unaffected.

A rule of thumb that prevents expensive mistakes: negatives do not act on close variants, synonyms or plurals in the way positive keywords do. If you block "job", you may still see "jobs" or "vacancy". Check Google's current explanation of negative matching before building a long list, and test with a few searches that you expect to be blocked.

### The danger of over-blocking

A negative keyword that is too broad can block valuable searches. If you add the single word `free` as a broad negative, you will also lose searches such as "free quote" and "free consultation", which may be exactly what your prospects type. Equally, blocking `cheap` could remove people who are price-conscious but ready to buy.

For each proposed negative, ask: "Could someone who would become a good customer ever type this?" If the answer is yes, use a narrower match type or a more specific phrase, or leave it alone.

### Level of negatives: ad group, campaign, list

- **Ad group level** is for keeping similar ad groups apart, so that a search about "website redesign" does not trigger your "new website" ad group. This is about routing, not blocking.
- **Campaign level** is for words that are irrelevant to the whole campaign.
- **Shared negative keyword lists** are for words that are irrelevant across the account, such as job and course terms. Maintaining one list and applying it to every campaign saves time and avoids gaps.

## Build a negative keyword list in layers

Rather than adding negatives one by one in a panic, build the structure deliberately.

### Layer 1: universal exclusions

These apply almost everywhere. Typical themes include careers and employment, education and training, free or DIY, and definitions or informational queries when you want buyers only. Review each word against your business before applying it. A training company, for instance, must not block "course".

### Layer 2: business-specific exclusions

These depend on what you sell. A website developer may exclude "template free download", "wordpress theme nulled" and "website builder free". A clinic may exclude queries about medicines it does not stock or treatments it does not provide. A D2C brand may exclude searches for competitors' products it is not comparing itself with.

### Layer 3: location exclusions

If you serve Pune and nearby areas, searches naming cities you do not serve can be excluded, although it is usually better to use location targeting settings correctly first. Review the location settings: Google's option to show ads to people "interested in" a location, not only physically in it, can bring in searches from elsewhere. Check which setting your campaigns use.

### Layer 4: ad group routing negatives

Add cross-negatives so that each search is shown the most relevant ad group. This helps keep your reports clean and your ad text relevant to the search.

## What broad match, AI Max and Performance Max change

The report matters more, not less, as Google steers advertisers towards broader matching and automation.

### Broad match with smart bidding

Broad match keywords can match searches that do not contain your words at all but that Google judges to be related. Google recommends combining broad match with automated bidding and good conversion tracking. In practice this means your search terms report will contain more surprises, and the negative keywords you add become the primary way to set limits. If you use broad match, review the report more often, not less.

### AI Max for Search

Google's AI Max for Search campaigns expands matching and can generate headlines and landing page selection. Our article on [AI Max migration](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-ai-max-migration-2026) explains what to check. For this topic, the key points are to look at the search terms and the landing pages that AI Max chooses, and to use negative keywords and URL exclusions where you need to control it. Check Google's help pages for the current controls, as they have been changing.

### Performance Max

Performance Max shows ads across Google's channels, and reporting for searches has been more limited than in standard search campaigns. Google has added some controls, including negative keywords at the account level for certain campaign types. Our article on [Performance Max reporting](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-performance-max-2026) covers what is visible. If a significant share of your budget goes into automated campaigns, ask your agency what is visible, what is excluded and how they check for irrelevant traffic.

## A weekly routine that takes under an hour

You do not need a complicated process. A steady habit, applied consistently, beats an occasional overhaul.

### Week by week

1. **Open the search terms report** for the last seven to fourteen days (and a 30-day view each month for patterns).
2. **Sort by cost.** Scan the top spenders first.
3. **Tag each term** using the four buckets above.
4. **Add negatives** at the right level and match type, noting why in a change log.
5. **Add winning terms** as exact or phrase keywords in the right ad group.
6. **Check the effect** the following week: has spend on those themes fallen? Have impressions and conversions on core terms held up?

### Keep a change log

Write down what you added and why. It sounds dull, but it protects you from two problems: an over-broad negative that quietly kills a good keyword, and an agency or employee change that leaves nobody knowing why a block exists. When results dip, the log lets you check whether a recent negative is the cause.

### Review the negatives themselves

Every quarter, review the negative lists for terms that block valuable traffic. Businesses change what they sell, and a negative that made sense a year ago may not now.

## Questions to ask your agency

If you pay a digital marketing agency in Pune to run your Google Ads, these questions will tell you whether the search terms report is part of their routine.

- How often do you review the search terms report, and can I see the change log?
- Which negative keyword lists are applied to my account, and who decides what goes into them?
- What proportion of spend goes to terms that do not match what we sell? (A good agency will have an honest answer, even if it is an estimate, and will explain how it is calculated.)
- How do you handle broad match and automated campaign types in terms of limiting irrelevant searches?
- How do you check that negatives are not blocking good traffic?
- What do you do about conversions that happen by phone or WhatsApp?
- Can I have access to the account, so I can see this myself?

The last question matters most. You should own the ad account and have at least read access, so the report is yours to check, not something you take on trust. Our [onboarding checklist for a digital marketing agency](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-onboarding-access-tracking-checklist-2026) explains account ownership in more detail, and our [monthly retainer guide](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-retainer-deliverables-reporting-2026) describes what a monthly report should contain.

## Worked example: a service business in Pune

The following is a hypothetical example to show the method, not a result from a client. Figures are deliberately not given.

A hypothetical home-renovation firm in Pune bids on "home renovation pune" and "flat renovation contractor". In its search terms report it finds:

- "home renovation loan" and "home renovation ideas" generate many clicks, no enquiries.
- "renovation contractor jobs pune" generates clicks, no enquiries.
- "flat renovation cost in pune" generates clicks and some enquiries.
- "kitchen renovation pune" generates enquiries, but the firm has no kitchen-only ad group.
- "home renovation in nashik" generates a few clicks; the firm does not serve Nashik.

The actions that follow are straightforward:

- Add `loan`, `jobs` and `ideas` as campaign-level phrase or broad negatives, after thinking about whether "ideas" could come from serious buyers (if the firm uses design ideas as a funnel, it might keep that).
- Add `nashik` as a negative, and check location settings.
- Keep "flat renovation cost in pune" and consider a landing page that answers the cost question honestly. Our article on [landing pages versus homepages for ads](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-landing-page-vs-homepage-ads-2026) helps with that decision.
- Create a kitchen ad group with its own ads and page, and cross-negative the term from the general group.

Within a few weeks, the firm should see the spend on the unproductive themes shrink and should be able to check the effect in its own account. We would not predict by how much.

## Common mistakes

- **Never opening the report**, and trusting a weekly summary instead.
- **Judging terms on too little data**, such as blocking a phrase after two clicks.
- **Adding broad negatives that remove good searches**, like "free" or "cheap" for a business that offers a free consultation.
- **Assuming negatives behave like positive keywords** with close variants and plurals.
- **Forgetting that conversion tracking is incomplete**, especially for calls and WhatsApp.
- **Not recording changes**, so nobody knows why traffic fell.
- **Blocking everything informational**, even though some informational searches become customers later.
- **Not owning the ad account**, so you cannot check any of this.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the search terms report in Google Ads?

It is a report listing the actual searches that triggered your ads, along with impressions, clicks, cost and conversions for each. It shows the real words people used, which often differ from the keywords you bid on, and is the main source of ideas for new keywords and for negative keywords.

### How often should I check my search terms report?

Weekly is a sensible habit for an account with steady spend, using a recent window of seven to fourteen days, with a longer monthly view to spot patterns. Accounts using broad match or automated campaign types usually deserve closer attention because the range of matched searches is wider.

### What are negative keywords in Google Ads?

They are words or phrases that stop your ad from showing for searches containing them. They can be exact, phrase or broad match, and applied at ad group, campaign or shared-list level. They do not behave like positive keywords with respect to close variants, so test them before relying on them.

### Can negative keywords hurt my campaign?

Yes. A negative that is too broad, such as blocking the word "free" when you offer a free consultation, can remove searches from people who are ready to buy. Check each proposed negative against what a good customer might type, use narrower match types when in doubt and keep a change log.

### Do I need negative keywords for Performance Max and AI Max?

Controls differ by campaign type and have been changing, so check Google's current documentation or ask your agency. In general, the more automation you allow, the more important it is to set limits and to look at the search and landing page reports that are available.
